summary: A reissue of the first BBN site status report, because the original RFC 235 had many typographical errors. It reports how often ARPANET hosts could be reached and which ones were excluded from daily test logins. It was replaced by RFC 252.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 240 reissues RFC 235 because the earlier report had extensive typographical errors. It includes daily test results for most Network Hosts and says BBN plans to report their status about once every two weeks.

questions: when did arpanet host reporting begin
what did the arpanet host status codes mean
subtitle: A corrected reissue of BBN's first ARPANET site status report

tldr.problem: RFC 235 had extensive typographical errors and needed a corrected reissue.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 240 republishes the report and presents daily host login-test results from the BBN prototype Terminal IMP.
tldr.outcome: It begins BBN's planned series of reports about most Network Hosts, approximately once every two weeks; RFC 252 later replaced it.

sections.title: Why the Report Was Reissued
sections.content:
The author reissued the first experimental site status report because RFC 235 contained extensive typographical errors. The note apologizes for the earlier document and says the author would try to do better.

RFC 240 says BBN will report on the status of most Network Hosts approximately once every two weeks. Information comes from conversations with people at each site and from test data.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a corrected copy of a report with many typing errors. BBN says it plans to publish host status reports about every two weeks.

sections.title: Daily Host Tests
sections.content:
The test data come from attempts to log into hosts that might be accessible to a network user. The attempts are made from the BBN prototype Terminal IMP at a random time each weekday. The tables report results from September 13 through September 24.

Five codes describe the result: O means open and accessible; D means dead or inaccessible from the test point; R means refused; T means timed out; and 1/2 O means the host opened a connection but then closed it or stopped responding.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables record the result of each attempted login. Their codes distinguish an accessible host from one that was unreachable, refused the request, timed out or only partly opened a connection.

sections.title: Excluded Hosts and Predictions
sections.content:
Some hosts are excluded from daily tests because they are not expected to act as servers for at least a month. Others are intended to be users only, including Terminal IMPs and the Network Control Center computer. The report also lists operator predictions about when hosts might become servers.

RFC 240 is later listed as obsoleted by RFC 252 in the unit metadata.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every host was tested: some were not expected to become servers soon, and some were intended only as users. RFC 252 later replaced this report.
